newsitem.title: USA: Newspaper profits seen strong in Q2.
newsitem.headline: Newspaper profits seen strong in Q2.

text.p: Newspaper companies, boosted by a healthy U.S. economy that has propelled strong advertising growth, are expected to post profit gains as high as 35 percent in the second quarter.
Newspaper chains are set to begin reporting results next week, and analysts observed that the industry is in the midst of a boom cycle.
"It should be a terrific quarter," said Ed Atorino, an analyst at Wasserstein Perrella. "These are the best times in decades ... We're in a long supercycle."

Analysts said classified revenues, which can account for more than 50 percent of total newspaper advertising, grew in the high single digits in the second quarter as help wanteds burgeoned. "Classifieds have been extremely strong," said Michael Kupinski at A.G. Edwards.

Retail advertising, long a poor performer for newspapers, was seen continuing its bounce back. "It now seems to be coming back," said Lauren Fine at Merrill Lynch. "For eight months in a row, retail ad volume has been growing."
National advertising also kept gaining, although at a more modest pace.

Financial services firms and computer makers beefed up ad campaigns, and marketing battles broke out within autos, pharmaceuticals and telecommunications companies, said Brian Oakes at Lehman Brothers.

The industry has also benefitted from lower newsprint prices compared to a year ago, but new hikes are seen. Newsprint manufacturers in March said they would seek a 15 percent raise in the price per ton, but they have been slow to come. "Look for an uptick," said Kupinski.
Analysts said second-half industry profit increases, while not as muscular as the first half, should reach 15-20 percent.
"Things are going to slow down," said Atorino. "There will be tough comparisons compared to last year."
One area that could buoy growth is classifieds. "Classified ads could surprise people, but it will be difficult on the recruitment side," said Fine.
Analysts noted classified revenues may slip in the second half versus a year ago, when the category jumped markedly after U.S. unemployment dipped below 5.5 percent.
Analysts were slightly jittery that if the U.S. economy slows down by next year, the heavily cyclical newspaper business would be one of the first to suffer.
"If we saw the economy stall out, and the job market starts to weaken, help wanteds will roll over," said Atorino. "Newspaper trends could start to slow pretty sharply."
Miles Groves, chief economist of the Newspaper Association of America, forecast that total newspaper ad expenditures will rise 5.4-5.7 percent in 1997 versus 6.3-6.5 percent in 1996.

Groves said classified spending should gain 8.1-8.5 percent this year versus 10.4-10.7 percent, and national advertising will slow to less than six percent versus about 10 percent, with no Olympics or political advertising this year. The retail slice should rise 3-3.5 percent versus 2.5 percent.
